title: Consumer Rights and Everyday Problems
summary: Fake products, misleading ads, refunds, hidden charges, and how to file a complaint as a buyer.

body.text: When you buy something or pay for a service, and it is broken, fake, late, or not what was promised, you have rights. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 protects buyers in shops, online, and over the phone.
Your main rights as a buyer

items: The right to be safe.
The right to know about the quality, quantity and price.
The right to choose.
The right to be heard and to get a solution.
The right to ask for compensation (money back) for unfair trade practices (dishonest ways of selling).
The right to consumer education (the right to learn about your rights).

body.text: Broken or fake products, and misleading ads (ads that tell lies)

items: If a product is broken or faulty, you can ask for a replacement, a repair, or your money back.
Selling fake goods, or advertising in a misleading way, is an 'unfair trade practice' (a dishonest selling trick) under this Act.
An ad must not tell lies about quality, quantity or results.

body.text: Bills, hidden charges and online shopping

items: A shop or restaurant must not add charges they did not tell you about. Ask for an itemised bill (a bill that lists each item and its price).
When you buy online, the seller must show the return, refund and warranty (guarantee) terms before you buy.
Keep the bill, the order ID, the warranty card, and all your chats or emails.

body.text: How to complain, step by step

items: First, complain to the seller in writing. If they do not fix it, go to a Consumer Commission (a special court for buyers).
District Commission (district-level court): claims up to 50 lakh rupees.
State Commission (state-level court): claims between 50 lakh and 2 crore rupees.
National Commission (national-level court): claims above 2 crore rupees.

body.text: For online shopping, the E-Commerce Rules, 2020 say sellers must clearly show the return, refund and warranty rules before you buy.
Usually, you have two years from the date of the problem to file a complaint.
You can file online on the e-Daakhil website. You can also call the National Consumer Helpline 1915 for help.
Mediation: a faster way to settle

items: The Act also allows mediation (a neutral person helps both sides agree) between you and the seller.
Mediation is meant to be a faster option than a full case.
If mediation does not work, your complaint can still go before the Commission.

body.text: Product liability: who pays when something goes wrong

items: Product liability (the duty to answer for harm) means a manufacturer or a seller can be held responsible for a defective product.
It also covers a deficient service (a service that was not done properly).
So both the maker and the seller can be answerable for the harm.

practicalSteps: Keep the bill, the order ID, the warranty card, and all your chats or emails.
Send a written complaint to the seller, and note the date.
Call 1915 or register on consumerhelpline.gov.in for help.
If the seller does not solve it, file on the e-Daakhil website.
exceptions: Products bought to resell, or for business use, are usually not covered.
Free services given without any payment may be outside this Act.
Some problems must first go to a sector regulator (the office that controls that industry), such as telecom or insurance.

faqs.a: Not always. Consumer Commissions are made to be simple. You can speak for yourself. Free help is available through consumer helplines and legal aid (free legal help).

faqs.q: Can I complain about a service, and not only a product?
faqs.a: Yes. This Act covers services like banking, insurance, telecom, housing and repairs.

misconceptions.myth: Online sellers are not responsible, because they are only a platform.
misconceptions.fact: The E-Commerce Rules, 2020 put duties on both the seller and the platform (the website that hosts the sellers).
